justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift from what I assessed as the current baseline level around 47, with each successive horizon incorporating a small positive trend assumption. At the one-day horizon, the estimate of 47.1 is essentially anchored to the present value with minimal expected movement, reflecting mean-reversion tendencies common in many financial or polling series over very short windows. At one week, I nudged the estimate slightly higher to 47.5, accounting for whatever underlying drift or momentum was embedded in recent data. At one month, the estimate of 48.0 continues that gentle upward trajectory, suggesting I anticipated a slow, persistent but modest directional move rather than any sharp discontinuity.

The confidence interval widths widen substantially as the horizon extends, which is a straightforward reflection of compounding uncertainty over time. At one day, the 90% interval spans roughly 3.2 units, capturing day-to-day noise but little else. By one week, the interval expands to about 6.6 units, incorporating the possibility of a meaningful data release, sentiment shift, or external shock within that window. At one month, the interval opens to 14 units, reflecting the reality that over four weeks, a wide range of macro events, policy changes, or structural shifts could meaningfully alter the trajectory in either direction. The widening also accounts for model uncertainty compounding across time.

There are specific tail risks that could push outcomes outside my stated intervals entirely. On the upside, a surprise positive catalyst — such as a better-than-expected economic report, a policy announcement, or a resolution of an ongoing uncertainty — could push the one-month figure well above 55. On the downside, an unexpected negative shock, such as a geopolitical escalation, a financial stress event, or a significant data miss, could drag the value below 41. These are by definition low-probability scenarios, but the one-month interval in particular is wide enough that I would assign meaningful probability mass to outcomes beyond its edges given how fat-tailed real-world distributions tend to be.

Finally, I should acknowledge that my estimates carry model risk — I may have miscalibrated the baseline level or the drift assumption, and if the true generating process has structural features I did not account for, my intervals could be systematically off-center rather than just wide or narrow. The one-day estimate is the most reliable simply because there is less time for such errors to accumulate, while the one-month estimate should be treated with the most skepticism and treated more as a directional signal than a precise prediction.
